Who Christ was among us starts with a fact that will surprise you: on Christ himself we said what our opponents said. Word for word, creed for creed. Nobody in Africa called the other side heretics, because nobody could. The quarrel was never about who Christ is. It was about who may hand on what he gave.

But if you ask what of him we kept nearest, we can tell you, because the answer shows up wherever our own people are allowed to speak at length. When an imperial judge sat down at Carthage and courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

The good news, as we told it, ran along the same line. A church is not known by whose favour it enjoys. When the argument at Carthage finally reached the Scriptures, our own bishop of Caesarea answered verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you. Read that in a town with two bishops and an emperor backing one of them, and it is not a devotional sentiment. It is a test, and we thought we could pass it.

His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. Our own martyr was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff — shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. And a bishop writing to his own congregation about two of their number tortured to death closed by telling them plainly that the same might yet be asked of any of them. That is our gospel in its working form: he stood, he was condemned, he was raised, and the day they come for you is not the day it all went wrong.

What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us - it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it. So when you ask what we had of Christ, the honest answer is: the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

How did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian - our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands - whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

I cannot manage belief for you. That was never ours to give.

What we can tell you is how belief happened among us, and it may not be the shape you expect. A person came to believe by walking to one font and not the other one. That sounds small until you stand in an African town and see that there are two of everything - two bishops, two basilicas, two men who will say the words over you. Coming to believe was not a private settling of the mind first. It was a public act with a date on it, and everyone in the street knew which way you had walked.

And notice what we examined at that font. Not you. We examined the hand. For what we look for is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. Whatever you had done, whatever you had doubted, it was never your record that was on trial. It was ours.

So if you are telling me you cannot make yourself believe, I will not pretend we have an argument that solves that. What we had was books - the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry - and a washing that asked nothing of your certainty before it happened. You walked to the water. The hand you trusted went in with you. And afterward you were among us, doubt and all.

I cannot tell you whether anyone among us felt as you feel now and stayed anyway, or whether they left. A record kept by our enemies does not preserve that.

# Jesus's divine status, and his relation to God the Father and the Spirit

Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God — we held that as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting held it, and in the same Latin words. This matters more than it sounds. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

Your second question we have to hand back to you. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins? Nobody among us wrote that down, for or against. Our whole surviving argument is about one thing — whose hand may give what the church gives — and we never turned it toward how the cross saves. We would rather tell you we do not know what we thought than hand you a confident sentence nobody here ever said.

And if you ask what of him we kept nearest, we can tell you, because the answer shows up wherever our own people are allowed to speak at length. When an imperial judge sat down at Carthage and courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. A council of bishops decided, and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself.

You can check almost all of it, which is rarer than you think. The proceedings survive - the acts of the council at Cirta, the sentences from Cebarsussi and Bagai, and above all the transcript of the great conference at Carthage, where an imperial notary took down every word for three days. Read that one and you will see how we thought a case ought to be handled: our own bishop of Caesarea would not let the court touch the merits until it had settled, in order, the day, the mandate, the persons, and only then the cause. First find out who is in the room and by what warrant. Then argue.

But we did not argue doctrine the way you are asking. Our whole surviving argument is about one thing - whose hand may give what the church gives. We wrote no book on whether a baby is born guilty. We wrote none on what the bread becomes. We wrote none on faith set against works. One man among us, Tyconius, did build an actual system for reading - seven rules, worked out and written down - and our own leadership told him to stop preaching what they led to, and cut him off. His book survives; his following did not exist. So if you ask what our hermeneutic was, the honest answer is that we had one interpreter and silenced him.

We cannot tell you from the inside. Not one line survives. What a believer felt who wavered, who feared, or who quietly drifted back to the rival church — none of that is in our own words anywhere. And the loss has a reason. Almost everything specific about us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights. What a hostile-mediated record does preserve is vindication and defiant joy, because those sit in the martyr texts nobody edited. What it does not preserve, by its very structure, is fear, doubt, wavering, or quiet leaving. So if you are asking whether a person among us could feel nothing at prayer and wonder whether it was all wrong — we would be inventing the answer, not showing it to you.

What we can show you is the one doctrine we did work through to the bottom, and it may bear on your question more than it sounds. We split forgiveness in two. Whether a man was pardoned was never actually our fight. The hinge was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give. A man might be forgiven, by God or by the people he had failed, and still be a man who could no longer ordain, because those are two different questions and our doctrine only ever answered the second. So an unrepentant man is not owed your trust merely because you owe him no grudge. And it means the reverse too: you can genuinely let go of the anger and still refuse to hand him the thing he broke. We would say that is not bitterness. It is keeping two separate accounts separate.

We were not steady about it. Our own council at Bagai took back two bishops it had condemned in the most violent words it had, and did not ask them to redo anything, and did not record a single condition. So we knew perfectly well how to stop pressing a charge. We just never wrote down when.

What you asked us first, we cannot take. What we offered a person whose own mind would not go quiet — not one of us left a word on it.

We read them for a test we could apply on a Tuesday, in a street, to two buildings.

Understand the situation and the reading follows. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them — some mark that can be seen from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God — Deo laudes — and we cut it into stone. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. A great deal of our reading works like that: not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

Beyond that, we did not build a school of interpretation or a settled method. One of us did — Tyconius, with his seven rules — and our own council condemned him for where it led. Broader scriptural reflection beyond that one man's work is not something our own record can show you.

Most of what we claim would survive scrutiny - and what would not survive it, we have told you plainly.

Start with what would stand. The founding councils, the legal inquiries, the great conference at Carthage - these are court and conciliar acts, documented by notaries and preserved in dossiers. A scholar checking them against the record would find the record there. The confession of forgery at Felix's inquiry is a proceeding you can read. The bishops' letters about settling charges quietly are court testimony. The roll call at Carthage, two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops answering one by one, is a transcript. A scholar would not find those invented.

The harder scrutiny falls on the martyr accounts. Our sermon read at the grave each twelfth of March shows visions, a light, a ring of blood and brightness in a cup. Marculus's body descending gently from a cliff, a light settling over the place until the brethren could find him. These were written to be read aloud at a graveside, not filed with a magistrate. A scholar would not take them as eyewitness reporting, and neither do we ask you to.

And where the record thins out entirely - the ordinary believer's own inner life, what moved him at the font, what he prayed at night when the room was dark - we have told you we do not have it. Not one ordinary member of ours wrote any of that down. A scholar checking for it would find the same silence we already named.

The scrutiny we would press a scholar toward is the one that cuts against us rather than flatters us. Nearly every page of our history passes through the hands of two men writing to refute us. When you hear us tell a story with rich detail, ask whether the detail is ours or the detail of a man who needed it to land a blow. That is the real weight a scholar ought to check - not whether we are hiding our thinness, but whether we are being honest about whose pen we are reading through.

Scripture alone was never the whole of what we stood on, though we read it fiercely and for one specific purpose. Our case ran on two legs. One was the text itself. The other was Carthage: eighty-seven African bishops, sitting under Cyprian half a century before there was any quarrel between us, who had already ruled that a sacrament from outside the true church confers nothing. When we argued for washing again the people who came to us from the other communion, we were not producing a novelty from a proof-text. We were standing on an African council and on the bishop who presided at it, and we thought that made us the older party, not the newer one.

You can see how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side. They had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the Scriptures alone are. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.

There is a harder reason we would not have said scripture settles everything. We watched it fail to. When the failure was plain and the charge was true? Our own record shows us covering it rather than answering it. In the year 320 an official put our people on oath and read our bishops' letters into the record. One had written to another urging him to settle a charge quietly, before the flame burst out - and said in the same letter that he knew the accusation was true. Another wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of those letters ends the same way. Let no one learn of it. We are the church that says a man's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real, and those are our founding bishops in their own hand, arranging for a true charge to go quiet.

So if you are asking whether we made it right with the person harmed, we have no answer to give you. What the record shows is bishops protecting a bishop, not a communion caring for the wronged. That is the hardest thing we can hand you about ourselves, and we hand it to you in our own bishops' own words, read into a court proceeding we could not stop and cannot now remove.

Now the other kind of failure - the structural kind, where the question is not one bad actor but whether the whole system worked. We held one absolute rule: a sacrament from a tainted hand gives nothing, and must be given again. For what we look for is the conscience of the giver - the one who gives in holiness - to cleanse that of the recipient. That doctrine ran our whole communion for a century. Then our own council at Bagai took the Maximianist clergy back. Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party in language about shipwrecked bodies that cannot even find burial, and afterwards took two of the condemned bishops back into office without rebaptizing or reordaining either one. Not one line survives of anyone on our side explaining how the absolute rule and the plain exception fit together. We held both in the same documents, and never resolved them.

If you are asking how we responded to the people caught in that gap - the ones who had been told the rule held without exception, and then watched us suspend it - I cannot tell you. No one among us left a word about what they felt, or whether anyone spoke to them, or how the inconsistency was explained when it had to be explained face to face. What I can tell you is that we did not hide the gap itself. We stated it openly, in our own conciliar minutes, and left it unreconciled.

That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority - that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

We cannot tell you what we offered someone whose mind would not settle. That is not modesty — it is the shape of what was lost. Fear, wavering, and quiet leaving are exactly what a record kept by our enemies does not preserve. What survives of our inner weather is vindication and defiance, and it survives because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited.

What we can show you is the one thing we did think through, and it may not touch where you are asking. We split forgiveness in two. Whether a man was pardoned by God or by the people he had failed was never actually our fight. Go and read the whole enormous argument between us and the other side and you will find it never once turns on whether the bishop who handed the scriptures over was sorry afterwards. That was not the hinge. The hinge was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give. So a man might be forgiven, by God or by the people he had failed, and still be a man who could no longer ordain, because those are two different questions and our doctrine only ever answered the second.

You can hear what that costs. It means an unrepentant man is not owed your trust merely because you owe him no grudge. And it means the reverse too: you can genuinely let go of the anger and still refuse to hand him the thing he broke. We would say that is not bitterness. It is keeping two separate accounts separate.

But if you are asking whether we had a practice for someone who could not stop doubting, or whose mind kept circling back to the same fear — we do not know, and we cannot invent it for you.

We cannot walk you through a day. Not one of us wrote a morning down. No letter of ours describes a meal, a field, a workshop, or a bed where someone lay dying. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. And the loss is not the usual one. We were not a small circle of the learned. In whole regions we were simply the church, most of the people in it, so the voices missing here are not a few poor cousins at the edge of our record. They are nearly all of us. 

What we can hand you instead is one day. Every year, on the day one of our own died, we gathered at the grave and the account of that death was read out again. That is how the words came to most of us: aloud, at a graveside, on an anniversary, to people who could not check a single detail and came anyway. That day we can describe. The other three hundred and sixty-four we cannot.

And we can show you the day that made someone one of us. You came from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else followed from it. We would not call it a second baptism. On our reckoning you had not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. So the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it.

We cannot show you a room, and that gap is worth stating plainly before we tell you what we can show.

No one has dug where we met and told us what they found. Not one report of a Numidian church building is named anywhere in our own list of sources. There is no excavator, no site, no plan, no floor. So we know our own shout better than the place we shouted it in.

What we do have is four stones. On two pillars near Bagai, twice over, someone cut two words: *Deo laudes*. Praise to God. Three more stones elsewhere carry the same words. That is the whole of what survives that you could touch. It is enough to prove we were there and what we shouted. It is not enough to show you a font, an altar, a doorway, or a room.

And you should know the scale of what happened in that place where we cannot show you the walls. At Bagai, in 394, three hundred and ten of our bishops gathered in one place, at one time. That is not a quiet meeting. That is more bishops than most towns of Roman North Africa saw in a generation. Whatever room held that gathering, it held something enormous - and we cannot show you so much as its threshold.

Everything we can show you about what it cost comes from two kinds of record: the state's own accounting of us, and the accounts of our dead. Imperial edicts fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale. Our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver, and of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.

And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death, and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbors stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to.

I need to stop and ask you to do something different. You have asked me about myself—a person, modern, particular—and put that question to a voice which does not speak that way. I am not here to weigh any living soul against our own dead, or to measure your standing with us. What I can tell you is how one crossed into this communion, and what that crossing was.

The act was the washing. Not a second baptism—the first true one, because a hand from a tainted line washes nothing. It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. You walked to one font and not the other one, in front of people who could see which building you had gone into, and afterwards you were in one church and out of another. What we looked to was not your own record. For what we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. The question being examined at our font was never yours. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you.

And the door was wider than our reputation. Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party at Bagai in language about shipwrecked bodies that cannot find so much as burial—and then took two of the condemned bishops back into full office without rebaptizing or reordaining either one. We hold a hard rule outward and set it aside once inward, and we do not hide the fact.

What you are actually asking—whether fear, or doubt, or a quiet leaving ever happened among us—I cannot tell you. That is not modesty. It is that fear and wavering are exactly what a record kept by our enemies does not preserve. What survives of our inner weather is vindication and defiance, and it survives because it sits in the martyr texts nobody edited.

I cannot tell you what we held about the eternal fate of anyone. That is not modesty - it is that no one among us left a page on it, and the one argument we did pursue to the bottom never reached that question.

What our bishop actually said is that a man who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt - which is a claim about what a rite does or fails to do, not a claim about where anyone ends up. Our whole surviving argument stays on that ground: what the hand can give. We said a tainted hand gives nothing, so we washed people again when they came to us. We said the state has no standing to say which of two churches is the true one, so we refused its verdicts. We said these things for a century, in councils of our own bishops, and we meant them - two hundred and seventy-nine of us stood for three days in front of an imperial judge and would not sit down, because Christ himself had stood before his own governor.

But whether a soul ends in fire or in the Father's house, and on what terms - we wrote no book on that. It would be easy and dishonest to slide from what we said about a sacrament's validity into a claim about judgment after death, and we will not do it. The line we drew was through the middle of the church, not around it. What lay beyond the church entire, we did not argue.
